Introduction

What we built, and why we built it this way

A console-based banking system where customers can hold an account, check their balance, and send money to another account.

The part we chose to do properly is the transfer. Instead of moving money the instant a user presses send, every transfer is stored as a pending request that an administrator reviews and approves.

The rule the whole system follows:
a balance changes in exactly one place in the code, and only an administrator can reach it.

Objectives

  • Store users, accounts and transfers in a real database
  • Keep two separate roles — customer and administrator
  • Make a transfer safe: both balances update together, or neither does
  • Keep a permanent record of every transfer and who approved it
  • Divide the work so four people can build it in parallel

Scope

A terminal application for one user at a time. No web interface, no networking — the focus is the data model and the transfer logic.

  • Say clearly why approval matters: it gives the project a real authorisation step and a real reason to make two database writes happen together.
  • If asked "why not transfer instantly?" — an instant transfer has nothing to approve and nothing to record. The pending model is what makes it a banking system rather than a calculator.

Technology

What we used, and why

PartChoiceReason
LanguageC++17The course language, with useful additions such as std::optional for “found or not found”.
DatabaseSQLite 3.45.1Real SQL in a single file. No server to install and no password to configure.
How it is includedBundled with the codeSQLite is one .c file inside our repository, so every team member builds the same version.
Build systemCMake + MinGWOne configuration file builds the project on any team member's machine.
Version controlGit & GitHubEach developer worked on a branch and merged through a pull request.

Not used, on purpose

  • No graphics library — the project is a terminal application
  • No external packages — everything needed is inside the repository
  • No networking — the database is a local file

One command to build. Clone the repository and run build.bat — there is nothing else to install.

  • If asked "why not MySQL?" — MySQL needs a server running and a username and password configured on every machine. SQLite is a single file, so the project runs anywhere immediately.
  • Zero setup was a real benefit: any team member could clone and build in one step.

Dev 1

Because the bottom two layers were finished first, the customer menu and the admin menu could be written at the same time by two different people — neither one had to write any SQL.

  • The key benefit to state: one small DB class holds all the SQLite code, so everyone else just calls simple functions like AccountModel::findByUserId().
  • Two extra things we did for safety: passwords are stored as a hash rather than plain text, and every SQL query passes its values as parameters instead of joining strings together.
Database design

Three tables

How they connect

  • Every user gets one account when they register
  • Every transfer records the account it came from and the account it went to
  • Every transfer keeps its status and the admin who decided it

Rejected transfers stay in the table. Nothing is deleted, so the history is a complete record of what was requested and what was decided.

  • New accounts open with $500 so the system can be demonstrated without building a deposit feature — mention this before anyone asks where the money came from.
  • Account numbers are generated from the user id in the format ACC000002, so they are unique and easy to read.
How a transfer works

Every transfer has three possible states

While it is pending

The transfer is visible to the customer in their history, but the balance has not moved.

When it is approved

The sender is debited and the receiver is credited together, and the transfer is marked approved.

When it is rejected

No balance changes at all. Only the status is updated, so the record of the request remains.

  • Emphasise the middle box: a pending transfer is only a record. No money has moved. That is the idea the next two slides demonstrate.
  • The program also checks the sender still has enough money at the moment of approval, not only when the transfer was requested.

The approval code

The one place a balance changes

if (action == 'A') {                    // admin approves

    // make sure the sender still has enough money
    if (from_account->balance < txn.amount) {
        cout << "Insufficient sender balance.";
        return;
    }

    db.execute("BEGIN;");                // start

    AccountModel::updateBalance(db, from_account->id,
                       from_account->balance - txn.amount);

    AccountModel::updateBalance(db, to_account->id,
                       to_account->balance + txn.amount);

    TransactionModel::updateStatus(db, txn.id, "approved");

    db.execute("COMMIT;");               // save all three together
}
else if (action == 'R') {               // admin rejects
    TransactionModel::updateStatus(db, txn.id, "rejected");
}

From src/admin/approval.cpp — shortened slightly to fit the slide

Why BEGIN and COMMIT

Approving a transfer needs three changes: take money from the sender, give it to the receiver, and mark the transfer approved.

Putting them between BEGIN and COMMIT tells the database to save all three or none of them. Money can never disappear halfway through.

Rejecting is much simpler — it only changes the status. There is nothing to give back, because the money never left.

  • Simple way to explain it: "if the computer switched off right after the money left Alice, it would be gone. BEGIN and COMMIT stop that — the database saves all three changes together or throws them all away."
  • The real code also has a try / catch that undoes the changes if anything fails. It was left out of the slide to keep it readable.

What registering does

  • Checks the username is not already taken
  • Stores the password as a hash, never as plain text
  • Creates the user, then creates their account
  • Gives the account a number and a $500 starting balance

A wrong password and an unknown username give the same message, so nobody can use the login screen to find out which usernames exist.

Highlighted text is what the user typed.

The list comes first

The program prints the pending transfers before asking for an ID, so the admin never has to guess a number.

All the details, then the choice

Both account numbers, the amount, the note and the date are shown before the approve or reject prompt.

This single keystroke is the only thing in the whole system that moves money.

  • Pause on Action: (A)pprove and connect it back: "behind this one letter is the BEGIN and COMMIT code we just looked at."
  • Both a and A work, and typing 0 cancels without changing anything.

Account : ACC000002 Balance : $350.00 ← settled ID Date From To Amount Status Note ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ 1 2026-08-04 10:39:47 ACC000002 (you) ACC000003 $150.00 approved rent for July

$500 − $150 = $350  and  $500 + $150 = $650

The total in the system is still $1,000. Money was moved, not created or lost — and the transfer is the same record, now marked approved.

  • The totals check is the clearest proof the transfer worked: $1,000 before, $1,000 after.
  • The administrator's row shows — for account and balance, because the admin has no bank account.
Handling wrong input

We tested every mistake a user can make

four wrong attempts in a row · alice
Enter recipient account number: ACC999999 Account not found. Enter recipient account number: ACC000002 Cannot send money to yourself. Enter recipient account number: ACC000003 Enter amount: 99999 Insufficient funds. Your balance is $350.00. Enter recipient account number: ACC000003 Enter amount: -50 Amount must be greater than zero.

The program never crashed and never closed — every mistake goes straight back to the menu.

If the user…The program…
types an account that does not existsays so before even asking for an amount
tries to send money to themselvesrefuses the transfer
enters zero or a negative amountrefuses the transfer
tries to send more than they haveshows their real balance and refuses
types letters instead of a numbersays the amount is invalid
picks a menu option that does not existasks again instead of closing
  • Note the order we chose: the recipient account is checked before asking for the amount, so the user is not asked to type a figure that will be thrown away.
  • The amount is checked in the C++ code and the database also refuses to store an amount of zero or less.

How we worked together

Branches and pull requests, not direct pushes

Rules we agreed on

  • Nobody pushes straight to main — always a branch and a pull request
  • Everyone writes a short log of what they built and why
  • The project must build with no errors before opening a pull request

Set up in the repository

  • GitHub Actions builds the project automatically on every push
  • A pull request template with a checklist
  • build.bat — one command to compile everything
  • Good honest detail to mention: when Dev 3's work was first merged, the files were in the wrong folders, so we moved them into the agreed structure and fixed how account numbers were shown in the history. It is written up in updatelog/dev3.md.
  • If asked what we would do differently: agree the folder layout before anyone opens a pull request, not during the review.
Conclusion

A working banking
system, built by
four people.

Customers can register, check their balance and request transfers. Administrators review those requests. When a transfer is approved, both balances change together and the decision is recorded permanently.

1,458
lines of C++ written together
3
tables holding every user, account and transfer

What we would add next

  • Deposit and withdraw, using the same approval steps
  • More than one account per customer — savings and current
  • Automatic approval for small transfers, so the admin only reviews large ones
  • Export a statement to a file for a chosen date range
  • Hide the password as it is typed

What we learned

Agreeing the database and the shared functions first is what allowed four people to build different parts of one program without getting in each other's way.
